cues.text: A Noblewoman's Early Piety
Born around 1303 to Birger Persson, a wealthy provincial judge of Uppland, and his devout wife Ingeborg, Bridget was raised with careful religious instruction from childhood.
Reportedly, she experienced her first visionary encounters with Christ while still a young girl, visions she kept largely private during the decades of her active married life that followed.
A relative on her mother's side, St. Ingrid, had died only a generation before Bridget's own birth, leaving the family with a living memory of sanctity already close at hand.
A Genuine and Loving Marriage
Married at a young age to Ulf Gudmarsson , prince of Närke, Bridget spent over twenty years in a marriage marked by real mutual affection and shared devotion.
The sources consistently describe it this way.
Together, they raised eight children, including her daughter St. Catherine of Sweden , who would later become her closest companion in her Roman years.

Both husband and wife undertook pilgrimages together, including one to Compostela, and their marriage stands as a rare and treasured medieval example of shared lay sanctity within an ordinary family life.
Widowhood and a New Calling
Ulf's death in 1344 marked a decisive turning point.
Bridget retired to live near the Cistercian monastery of Alvastra, where her visionary experiences intensified dramatically after continuing quietly through her married years.
These experiences culminated in a sustained series of revelations she dictated to her confessor, who translated her spoken Swedish into Latin for wider circulation across Christian Europe.
Among these revelations, Bridget understood a specific command to found a new religious order.
She would not be able to fulfill the instruction until near the very end of her long life.
The resulting Bridgettine order, established at Vadstena, was distinctive for housing both men and women within a single monastic community under a shared rule.
A Prophetic Voice in Rome
In 1349, Bridget traveled to Rome, seeking papal confirmation for her new religious order and a wider platform for her larger mission.
She understood that mission as the moral and spiritual reform of a Church she judged to be in genuine crisis.

She remained in Rome, aside from occasional pilgrimages, for the rest of her life, becoming known throughout the city for both her personal charity toward the poor and the sick and her increasingly forceful public advocacy for Church reform.
Above all, Bridget pressed with persistence that bordered on the relentless for the pope—resident for decades at Avignon in France rather than Rome—to return the papacy to its rightful seat.
She pursued this campaign through direct correspondence and personal appeal to successive popes across the final decades of her life.
A Final Pilgrimage
In 1372, already an elderly woman, Bridget undertook a final demanding pilgrimage to the Holy Land, spurred, she believed, by a fresh vision.

She returned to Rome only to fall ill and die there on 23 July 1373, at seventy years old, having spent nearly a quarter century pursuing her twin missions of founding her order and reforming a wandering Church.
Legacy
Bridget's tireless advocacy for the papacy's return to Rome bore fruit only a few years after her death.
Pope Gregory XI finally left Avignon for Rome in 1377.
Her own daughter Catherine and, not long after, St. Catherine of Siena would continue to press for that return in the years immediately following.
Canonized in 1391 and declared one of the patron saints of Europe by Pope John Paul II in 1999, Bridget remains a singular figure in the Church's history.
Alongside Catherine of Siena and Bridget of Sweden's own patronage, she was declared one of Europe's patron saints.
A wife, mother, mystic, and reformer, her visions never remained merely private, but drove her, across decades of determined labor, to help reshape the very geography of the papacy itself.
